scout.saturation:
The broad searches belong to big channels: How Money Works (1.77M subs), Economics Explained (2.89M), Johnny Harris (8.02M), The Infographics Show (15.5M), Bloomberg Originals (5.23M), LITTLE BIT BETTER (1.44M), Maxinomics (848K), Primate Economics (577K, cartoon 'explained with bananas'), Crayon Capital (317K) and MonkeyExplains (261K). Their videos mostly run at 0.02x to 3x, so they win on subscribers, not packaging.

Even so, YouTube is clearly pushing new channels here. Of the 62 niche outliers at 10x or more, 43 come from channels under 10K subscribers and 58 from channels under 50K, on 54 different channels.

The stick-figure version, though, is flooded and templated:
- 39 stick-labelled finance explainers on 30 channels have a median of 178 views, and only one has 10K+ (from an 826K-subscriber channel).
- 18 AI 'make stickman finance videos' tutorials have 3.08M views between them, so more clones are coming.
- Copies of hit titles fail: 17 of 18 laundering copies posted within 14 days of the hit got under 1,000 views, and the $40T debt and wealth-ladder copies did the same.

So there is room for a new channel. A clone gets nothing; what wins is an original angle on a specific subject, sold on the topic rather than the stick-figure look.
gaps: 'The Economics of Owning ONE ___' in English for everyday assets and small businesses. Outliers on 15+ channels (semi-truck 165.6x, holding company 86x, EV 66x, hotel 23x), each subject covered by only 1 or 2 videos, and no stick-figure channel in the data has done the format.

'How [everyday product] makes money even if you ___': credit cards when you pay in full (320x on 436 subs) was the only video of its kind in the results; banks got 18.6x on 1,520 subs. The 'how credit card companies make money' search returned 0 videos this year.
'Where do you rank' from official data for ages other than 60+: all 6 Fed-data outliers (17.6x to 132.7x) target retirees, and no version for younger adults appeared.

Specific-cause cost of living (one product, one cause or one comparison, such as AI costs, McDonald's or a Porsche 911) instead of the crowded generic 'why is everything so expensive' and 'why you feel broke', where most small-channel videos this month got under 1,000 views.
Money history and objects (banknotes 176x, dollar symbols 14x, the origin of money 28x): only a handful of videos in the results.
Single-company money stories outside Costco (business model, rise and fall): FinXplain's Blinkit at 211x and Delta at 9.6x, with few English competitors per company.
Fresh twists on the complete-set and ladder format (Rich Kit's first homes by income at 20.6x) rather than the now-saturated generic 'every level of wealth'.
scout.thumbnail_notes:
Winners in sheet-year.png and sheet-month.png:
1. One round-headed stick or cartoon figure, usually in a suit, caught mid-reaction (sweating, screaming, smirking), in the centre or right third.
2. A huge number or a 2 to 4 word question in heavy outlined type, usually at top left: "$40 TRILLION", "$0 TAX", "$1T interest/year", "80% GO BROKE?", "WHO GETS PAID? Not China.", "WHO HAS A PENSION?", "IS IT WORTH IT", "2008 AGAIN?", "WHO WINS FROM INFLATION?". The text adds a hook instead of repeating the title.
3. One real-world anchor drawn in the same flat style: the White House with a flag, a world map stamped DEBT, a card terminal, a seesaw, a Costco store.
4. Flat, bright, uncluttered backgrounds (yellow, red, blue, green). Collapse topics use dark or fire backgrounds instead.
5. Split or contrast frames: "$0 | $40 TRILLION", "YOU EARN 0.38% / YOU PAY 21%", "SELL → $0 TAX".
6. Labelled grids and ladders for complete-set topics: 4 captioned panels (OLD MONEY / NEW MONEY / CRYPTO RICH / QUIET MILLIONAIRE; FIXER-UPPER / STUCK AT 3% / HOUSE POOR / OLD MONEY), a rank staircase ("WHERE DO YOU RANK?"), icon grids, a banknote grid.
7. Five 'Economics of Owning' channels share one template: "SO YOU WANT TO OWN/BUY A ___" in black on white, a red underline and a photo or illustration of the asset.

The low-performer sheet (sheet-lowperf-month.png, 273 to 901 views) uses the same round-head figures and the same "$40 TRILLION" and Trump-with-money-bag compositions. Near-identical copies of PENNY's "$0 | $40 TRILLION" (Rise With Odn, 758 views) and Billionaire Files' "-$40 TRILLION" (Money Stickman, 603 views) failed. The style is the minimum; topic choice, a fresh angle and timing made the difference.

patterns.pattern: TOPIC: AI bubble, meaning 'who goes bankrupt first' and AI companies falling. Demand is real this month, but these are forward-looking market predictions, not documented rise-and-fall stories, and they read as financial speculation or advice. That is a monetization and brand-safety risk for a documentary channel. If used at all, cover only collapses that have already happened (for example Character.AI or the metaverse spend) and never predictions.

patterns.pattern: TITLE/FORMAT: Numbered or 'Every [category] that…' lists work (restaurant chains, phones, stores, dealership chains, computer brands). scout.saturation: Big outlets are present but are not the ones being pushed. Business Insider's 'Rise And Fall Of' series (1.9M to 2.9M views), WSJ 'What Went Wrong', Bloomberg Originals (5.23M subs), CNBC (4.18M), Think School (6.62M), ColdFusion (5.26M) and The Infographics Show (15.5M) all show up, but at 0.07x to 2x their subscriber counts. Mid-size business-documentary channels do the same: Logically Answered (930K) 1.61x, Bright Sun Films (1.66M) 0.44x, Modern MBA (848K) 0.25x, Moon (1.8M) 0.28-1.16x, Wendigang (991K) 0.71-2.58x, Weird History Food (786K) 0.18-0.98x. The highest ratios almost all come from channels under 30K subs: Haul Drive 93, MAXIMUS 2,330, Thingform 4,330, Fortune & Fall 6,340, Hungerwise 9,470, Nimbus 14,500, Build Inc. 26,900. So YouTube is actively distributing new channels' packaging in this niche, and no single giant owns it. The crowding is at the bottom instead. Low-effort faceless uploads flood the popular sub-topics: 18 of 20 results for 'restaurant chain that destroyed itself' and 18 of 20 for 'startup fraud collapse' (this month) were under 5,000 views. About 10 Theranos videos uploaded this month all sit under 1,500 views, and 13 of 18 'electronics brand what happened' results this month were under 5,000. The carmaker 'Is Losing Everything' look is copied across several small channels in 30 days. Room for a new channel exists, but only for distinct, well-researched episodes, not clones. One query ('rise and fall of company', month) returned no results.
gaps: Regional and industrial collapses outside the US mega-brands (UK haulage and manufacturing, Canadian and US company towns, South African and Australian chains). These have the highest ratios in the data: Eddie Stobart 911.68x on 93 subs, with three independent outliers; South African dealership chains 84.37x and 20.68x; Chatham, Ontario 31.55x; Reliant 13.52x. Each story has only one to three videos.

Cross-border failure ('Why X failed in [country]' or 'lost [market] to [rival]'): Walmart in Europe 159.52x on 4,330 subs, Japanese cars losing Thailand 213.9x on 48 subs, BMW's China mistake 115.11x. Few competing videos turned up.

Fad and consumer brands while the story is live: Labubu reached 2.26M views at 356.81x, and the only other sizeable Labubu video in the data was Statrys at 3.72x. In fashion and consumer collapses, Build Inc. (Yeezy, Ed Hardy, TOMS at 14-20x) is nearly alone with a consistent series.

Single restaurant chains with one concrete decision, rather than the now-cloned 'Every restaurant chain' lists: Why KFC Dumped Pepsi 158.32x on 2,010 subs, Wendy's store closures 148.96x, Sriracha owner 19.95x, Crumbl 10.95x on 1.24M views.

Well-made heritage electronics and hi-fi histories: well-made versions win (Philips 34.46x at 520K views, Aiwa 22.67x, computer brands 66.84x at 1.58M), while dozens of thin uploads on the same brands sit at near-zero views. The gap is quality, not the topic.
For-profit education collapses (weak evidence, two videos): Everest College 47.61x at 490K views on 10,300 subs; Byju's 221.72x on a 50-sub channel.
scout.thumbnail_notes: Both sheets (24 on-niche outliers each, this year and this month) show the same recipe. (1) The hero is the company's own recognisable asset, not a presenter: the logo on the HQ or dealership (Honda, Stellantis, BMW, Volvo, Nissan, Walmart), the product (Labubu doll, Sriracha bottle, Yeezy and TOMS shoes, Ed Hardy shirt, Tata Nano, a phone line-up), or the depot or factory (Eddie Stobart, Philips, JVC, Reliant, Chatham). Faces appear on only about 5 of 48 thumbnails (Eddie Stobart composite, Byju's founder, Wendy's founder, Zuckerberg next to his avatar, one presenter). (2) One to three words of giant block capitals add a verdict or a loss figure that the title doesn't repeat: "IT'S OVER" in quotes (Honda, Stellantis, BMW, Volvo, Nissan, and rooked's fast-food boxes), WORTHLESS NOW, WHAT WENT WRONG?, DIED, DISGRACE, IRREVERSIBLE, GAME OVER, BUILT TO FAIL, LOST ITS SOUL, BYE BYE..., HOW TO KILL A BRAND, $533M VANISHED, $47B GONE, $80B WASTED, -99.3% IN 5 YEARS, 800 GONE. (3) Decay cues: fire and flames behind or on the product (the carmaker set, Jaguar, Yeezy, TOMS, Ed Hardy, Nano), a red falling arrow or chart line (Labubu, Byju's, $47B, Sriracha, Europe cars), or abandoned overgrown buildings under grey sky (Eddie Stobart x2, Philips, JVC, the New England drive-in, Chatham). (4) Two visual families work: a loud one (black, red and fire with white or yellow heavy sans) for current and newsy stories, and a quiet heritage one (muted derelict factory with a gold or cream serif title, as on Fallen Hi-Fi, Once Britain and Canada's Lost Legacy) for evergreen industrial and hi-fi histories. (5) List videos use a clean grid of logos on white (Hungerwise's 8 chain logos, copied by rooked.) or a product line-up (Droid Sage's phones). (6) Several winners look AI-composited (the Eddie Stobart executive, the Coca-Cola illustration, Labubu). MAXIMUS and Nimbus share a near-identical template. Copy the principles, never the layout, and avoid 'IT'S OVER'-style verdicts on companies that are still operating unless the video proves them.
